warmup.q: Limits has static final int MAX_CAST = 12;, static final Integer CAP = 12; and a static {} block that prints "init". Another class prints Limits.MAX_CAST, then Limits.CAP. When does "init" appear?
options: Before the first value, because touching any member of a class runs its start-up code
Between the two values: reading MAX_CAST doesn't run Limits's start-up code, reading CAP does
Never, because both fields are static final
warmup.why: MAX_CAST is a constant variable: a static final primitive or String whose value the compiler can work out. javac copies 12 into the caller's class file, so at run time the caller never touches Limits. CAP is boxed (Integer.valueOf runs), so it isn't a constant, and reading it runs Limits's static initializer. A class runs that code at most once, so "init" can't print twice. The section on the three steps shows it in a demo.

opening:
Picture a small theatre company putting on a play. Props are fetched only when a scene first needs them. Before making a new crown, the stage manager asks the head of props whether the company has one. And before the first night there is one dress rehearsal, held exactly once.

The JVM, the program that runs your compiled Java and Kotlin, works the same way. It brings in each class only when some code first needs it, through objects called class loaders, and it runs the class's start-up code once. Most days you never notice. Then a program that worked for months tells the violinist to arrive 0 minutes before curtain-up. Or a log fills with NoClassDefFoundError for a class that is sitting right there in the jar.

Both traps are easy to walk into, because nothing in the source says when its code runs. Part 3 ended with an API that Java and Kotlin callers share; Part 4 goes inside the JVM. In this lesson, we'll meet its three class loaders, follow one class from loading to its first run, and load a class twice on purpose. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a theatre that fetches each prop only when a scene needs it, asks the head of props first, and holds one dress rehearsal. The JVM does the same: three loaders that ask their parents first, and three steps of which only the last runs your code. Its <clinit> runs once, in order, under a lock, and never again.

Now open a project of yours and search for static final fields whose initializer calls a method, such as load(, read, parse or getProperty. Each one runs in a rehearsal you can't hold twice.

Next, we'll open a class file and read the instructions inside <clinit> and every other method: what does the compiler really write down?

sections.h: Three class loaders, and why each asks its parent first
sections.html:
Your compiled program is a pile of class files in folders and jars (a jar is a zip file of class files). The JVM reads none of them until some code needs one. The object that finds a class's bytes and turns them into a Class the JVM can run is a class loader.

Let's set the theatre up properly before we lean on it. The building has its own store of things every show needs, such as chairs and the curtain. The company has a props department for rarer items. And each production has a stage manager who looks after the props made for that show. A class loader is one of these three people. A class is a prop, and its class file is the drawing the prop is made from.

Ask three classes who loaded them, and you get three answers. ShowProgram here is our own main class:

Java
System.out.println(String.class.getClassLoader());               // null
System.out.println(java.sql.Connection.class.getClassLoader());   // ...ClassLoaders$PlatformClassLoader@<hash>
System.out.println(ShowProgram.class.getClassLoader());          // ...ClassLoaders$AppClassLoader@<hash>
Kotlin
println(String::class.java.classLoader)                // null
println(java.sql.Connection::class.java.classLoader)   // ...ClassLoaders$PlatformClassLoader@<hash>
println(ShowProgram::class.java.classLoader)           // ...ClassLoaders$AppClassLoader@<hash>

The JDK has three built-in class loaders. The bootstrap loader is part of the JVM itself and loads java.base, the module that holds String, List and the other basics. A module is a named group of packages. The bootstrap loader has no Java object of its own, so getClassLoader() returns null. The building's store has no name badge.

The platform loader loads the rest of the JDK's modules, such as java.sql for databases: that's the props department. The app loader loads your class path, the list of folders and jars you give the java command: your own code and every library you added, Kotlin's standard library included. That's the stage manager.

Each loader has a parent. The app loader's parent is the platform loader, and the platform loader's parent is the bootstrap loader. When code asks a loader for a class, the default loadClass method does three things in order:

  1. It checks whether it already loaded that name (findLoadedClass).
  2. If not, it asks its parent, which asks its own parent first.
  3. Only when every parent says no does it look for the class itself (findClass).

That's the stage manager asking the head of props, who asks the building's store, before anyone makes a new crown. It's called parent-first delegation. It's why java.lang.String always comes from the bootstrap loader, even if some jar on your class path holds a class with that very name. A stray jar can't replace a JDK class.

The loader that finally builds the class, by calling defineClass, is its defining loader, and it is part of the class's identity. At run time a class is the pair (name, defining loader). The name is the binary name, the full name such as theatre.Scene, or theatre.Scene$Cue for a class nested inside Scene. Two loaders can each define a class with the same name, and the last section shows what that does to a cast.

Kotlin adds nothing special here. kotlin.Unit is an ordinary class in an ordinary jar, so the app loader loads it like any other library class.

Every loader asks its parent first. That's why the JDK's own classes always win.

So far, "loading a class" has sounded like one event. Inside the JVM it's three.

steps: Before you run it, write down the loader and the module you expect for String, java.sql.Connection, the demo class itself and kotlin.Unit.
Run LoaderTour from the labs/ folder with the command below, then run the Kotlin twin.

"bootstrap" : l.getName(), c.getModule().getName()); } }

alt.html: package workbench.bytecode.l01 import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory /** Which loader defined which class, and the chain a class-loading request walks up. */ fun main() { show(String::class.java) // java.lang.String, in java.base show(java.sql.Connection::class.java) // java.sql, a platform module show(TourMarker::class.java) // this program, on the class path show(Unit::class.java) // the Kotlin standard library jar, also on the class path val chain = generateSequence(TourMarker::class.java.classLoader) { it.parent } .joinToString("") { "${it.name} -> " } println("delegation chain: ${chain}bootstrap (null)") println("classes loaded so far: ${ManagementFactory.getClassLoadingMXBean().loadedClassCount}") } private class TourMarker private fun show(c: Class<*>) { val l = c.classLoader println("%-34s loader=%-9s module=%s".format(c.name, l?.name ?: "bootstrap", c.module.name)) }

try.expect: String has the bootstrap loader (printed as null, shown here as bootstrap) in java.base, and java.sql.Connection has the platform loader in java.sql. The demo class and kotlin.Unit both have the app loader and no module name (module=null), because the class path is one unnamed module. The chain is app -> platform -> bootstrap. On JDK 25 one run counted 948 loaded classes for Java and 986 for Kotlin: the Kotlin program touches more of its standard library, and every class it touches is loaded.

sections.h: Loading, linking and initialization: three steps, and only the last runs your code
sections.html:
Loading a class and running its start-up code are separate events, and they can happen far apart. Chapter 5 of the JVM specification, the document that says how every JVM must behave, splits the work into three steps. HotSpot, the JVM inside the JDK you installed, runs each step as late as it is allowed to.

A new prop goes through the same three steps. Someone fetches it. Before any scene uses it, the crew checks it, gives it a labelled spot on the props table and fills in the cue sheet that says where it's needed. Last comes the dress rehearsal, the only step that puts actors on stage.

  1. Loading finds the bytes, in a folder, a jar, or made in memory, and turns them into a Class object with defineClass. That's fetching the prop.
  2. Linking gets the class ready, in three parts. Verification checks that the bytecode, the instructions the compiler wrote into the class file (the next lesson reads them), is type-safe: no instruction treats a number as a string. Preparation creates the static fields and sets them to their defaults, 0, false or null: an empty, labelled spot on the table. Resolution turns the names the class uses, such as "method fire in class Lights", into direct links. It may do that one name at a time, the first time each is used.
  3. Initialization runs the class's static initializer, which javac names <clinit> ("class init"): every static field initializer and static {} block, top to bottom. That's the dress rehearsal.

Two small experiments show the gaps between the steps. A generated class with broken bytecode was accepted by defineClass on JDK 25, and the VerifyError came only when code first asked for its methods. A class that referred to a deleted Helper class loaded and ran fine. It failed with NoClassDefFoundError only when the branch that used Helper ran.

That second experiment is where the picture breaks. A real crew checks a whole prop before the show. The JVM may fill in the cross-references lazily, one name at a time, and never at all for code that never runs.

Initialization is the step your code can see, and its triggers are exact. Section 12.4.1 of the Java Language Specification lists them: creating an instance, calling a static method, assigning a static field, or reading a static field that isn't a constant variable. Initializing a class first initializes its superclass. Reflection counts too: code that looks up classes and their members by name while the program runs, such as Class.forName(name).

These do not initialize a class:

  • reading a static final primitive or String whose value the compiler can work out, because javac copied the value into your class file;
  • Limits.class, new Limits[3] and Class.forName(name, false, loader);
  • reading an inherited static field through a subclass: Child.parentValue initializes only Parent, the class that declares the field.

The constant rule surprises people most, and it's the warm-up question. static final int MAX_CAST = 12 is a constant variable. static final Integer CAP = 12 is not, because boxing calls Integer.valueOf. Reading the first leaves Limits alone, and reading the second runs <clinit>. Kotlin draws the same line between const val and a plain val.

Loading isn't initialization. Only the first real use runs <clinit>.

So <clinit> runs late, and it runs once. Those two facts are behind three real bugs, and the call sheet has the first one.

try.title: The initialization puzzle
steps: Read InitPuzzle (or InitPuzzle.kt). For each of the eight steps, write down whether a <clinit> line prints after it, and which one.
Run it and check your list.
Change CAP to static final int CAP = 12; (in Kotlin, make it const val). Predict step 4, then run it again.

code.title: InitPuzzle.java
code.html: package workbench.bytecode.l01; /** Predict which steps run a static initializer. Each <clinit> prints one indented line. */ public class InitPuzzle { static class Parent { static int parentValue = 1; static { System.out.println(" Parent.<clinit>"); } } static class Child extends Parent { static { System.out.println(" Child.<clinit>"); } } static class Limits { static final int MAX_CAST = 12; // a constant variable: javac copies 12 into callers static final Integer CAP = 12; // boxed, so not a constant variable static { System.out.println(" Limits.<clinit>"); } } static class Lazy { static { System.out.println(" Lazy.<clinit>"); } static void touch() {} } interface Step { void run() throws Exception; } static void step(String what, Step s) throws Exception { System.out.println(what); s.run(); } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { step("1. read Child.parentValue", () -> { int v = Child.parentValue; }); step("2. new Child()", () -> new Child()); step("3. read Limits.MAX_CAST", () -> { int v = Limits.MAX_CAST; }); step("4. read Limits.CAP", () -> { Integer v = Limits.CAP; }); step("5. new Lazy[3]", () -> { Lazy[] a = new Lazy[3]; }); step("6. Lazy.class", () -> { Class<?> c = Lazy.class; }); step("7. Class.forName(name, false, loader)", () -> Class.forName("workbench.bytecode.l01.InitPuzzle$Lazy", false, InitPuzzle.class.getClassLoader())); step("8. Lazy.touch()", Lazy::touch); } }

alt.title: InitPuzzle.kt
alt.html: package workbench.bytecode.l01 // Kotlin has no static fields of its own. An `object` and a companion object compile to a // class with a static initializer, so the same JVM rules decide when the init blocks run. open class KParent { companion object { @JvmField var parentValue = 1 init { println(" KParent.<clinit>") } } } class KChild : KParent() { companion object { init { println(" KChild.<clinit>") } } } object KLimits { const val MAX_CAST = 12 // a constant: kotlinc copies 12 into callers val CAP: Int = 12 // a property: reading it goes through KLimits init { println(" KLimits.<clinit>") } } object KLazy { init { println(" KLazy.<clinit>") } fun touch() {} } private fun step(what: String, s: () -> Any?) { println(what) s() } /** Predict which steps run a static initializer. Each one prints one indented line. */ fun main() { step("1. read KParent.parentValue") { KParent.parentValue } step("2. KChild()") { KChild() } step("3. read KLimits.MAX_CAST") { KLimits.MAX_CAST } step("4. read KLimits.CAP") { KLimits.CAP } step("5. arrayOfNulls<KLazy>(3)") { arrayOfNulls<KLazy>(3) } step("6. KLazy::class.java") { KLazy::class.java } step("7. Class.forName(name, false, loader)") { Class.forName("workbench.bytecode.l01.KLazy", false, KLazy::class.java.classLoader) } step("8. KLazy.touch()") { KLazy.touch() } }

try.expect: Step 1 prints only Parent.<clinit>, because the field belongs to Parent. Step 2 prints only Child.<clinit>, because Parent is already done. Step 4 prints Limits.<clinit>, step 8 prints Lazy.<clinit>, and steps 3, 5, 6 and 7 print nothing. After the change, step 4 prints nothing too, and Limits is never initialized at all. The Kotlin twin shows the same pattern with KParent, KChild, KLimits and KLazy.

sections.h: The dress rehearsal runs once: order, failure and deadlock
sections.html:
The show program keeps a call sheet: the list that tells each player how many minutes before curtain-up to arrive. Leads come 90 minutes early and the chorus 45, and anyone else gets a default of 60, read from a setting. Here it is, trimmed from the lab's starting code:

Java
// Naive: the shared instance is built too early
public final class CallSheet {
    private static final Map<String, Integer> MINUTES_BY_ROLE = Map.of("LEAD", 90, "CHORUS", 45);
    public static final CallSheet INSTANCE = new CallSheet();       // runs here
    private static final int DEFAULT_MINUTES =
            Integer.parseInt(System.getProperty("calls.default.minutes", "60"));

    private final int fallbackMinutes = DEFAULT_MINUTES;            // still 0 here
}
Kotlin
// Naive: the shared instance is built too early
class CallSheet private constructor() {
    val fallbackMinutes = DEFAULT_MINUTES                           // still 0 here

    companion object {
        private val MINUTES_BY_ROLE = mapOf("LEAD" to 90, "CHORUS" to 45)
        @JvmField val INSTANCE = CallSheet()                        // runs here
        private val DEFAULT_MINUTES = System.getProperty("calls.default.minutes", "60").toInt()
    }
}

Ask it about the violinist, a role the table doesn't list, and the lab's test reports:

CallSheet: an unlisted role gets the 60-minute default, not 0 FAILED
    expected: 60
     but was: 0

Nothing threw. The violinist is now part of the overture. The JVM did exactly what the source says: <clinit> runs top to bottom, and the INSTANCE line builds the object before the next line has set DEFAULT_MINUTES. The constructor reads that field while it still holds the 0 from preparation. Picture a dress rehearsal that plays the scenes in script order, even when scene 2 needs a prop that only scene 3 brings on.

With a constant initializer (= 60) the bug would disappear, because javac copies a constant into the code that reads it. That's why this bug tends to arrive on the day someone makes a constant configurable. You'll fix it in the lab.

<clinit> has two more properties, and both cause real outages. It runs once, and a failure is permanent. Here's a class that reads a script file while it initializes:

Java
static class Script {
    static final String TEXT = load(Path.of("hamlet.txt"));   // runs inside <clinit>

    static String load(Path p) {
        if (!Files.exists(p)) throw new IllegalStateException("script file missing: " + p);
        return "To be, or not to be";
    }
}
Kotlin
object Script {
    val TEXT: String = load(Path.of("hamlet.txt"))           // runs inside <clinit>

    fun load(p: Path): String {
        check(Files.exists(p)) { "script file missing: $p" }
        return "To be, or not to be"
    }
}

With the file missing, a small program touched Script.TEXT three times. On JDK 25 it printed:

1: java.lang.ExceptionInInitializerError
   cause: java.lang.IllegalStateException: script file missing: hamlet.txt
2: java.lang.NoClassDefFoundError: Could not initialize class Rehearsal$Script
   cause: java.lang.ExceptionInInitializerError: Exception java.lang.IllegalStateException: script file missing: hamlet.txt [in thread "main"]
3: java.lang.NoClassDefFoundError: Could not initialize class Rehearsal$Script
   cause: ...the same as 2

The first use gets ExceptionInInitializerError. The JVM marks the class as failed, and every later use, from any thread, gets NoClassDefFoundError: Could not initialize class. Since JDK 21 that error's cause names the first exception and the thread it happened in. A theatre would hold the dress rehearsal again tomorrow. The JVM never tries again, for as long as that class loader lives, and that's where the picture breaks. In a long log you often see the NoClassDefFoundError hundreds of times, and the real cause once, near the top.

The third property is that <clinit> runs under a lock. One thread runs it, and every other thread that needs the class waits. That lock is what made the holder idiom in the memory model track safe, and it can also deadlock: two threads each wait for something the other holds, for ever. In the Try it below, Cast's initializer reads Costumes, Costumes's initializer reads Cast, and two threads start one each. Each thread holds one class's lock and waits for the other's.

Both threads report RUNNABLE, the most hopeful state a stuck thread can show. ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads(), the JDK's deadlock detector, finds nothing. jstack, a JDK tool that prints every thread's stack, shows this on JDK 25:

"cast" #21 ... in Object.wait()
   java.lang.Thread.State: RUNNABLE
	at workbench.bytecode.l01.InitDeadlockDemo$Cast.<clinit>(InitDeadlockDemo.java:10)
	- waiting on the Class initialization monitor for workbench.bytecode.l01.InitDeadlockDemo$Costumes

There's no "Found one Java-level deadlock" section. When a program hangs at start-up, search the dump for Class initialization monitor.

Keep static initializers boring: constants and small fixed tables only.

Reading files, calling other computers and reading other classes' statics belong in ordinary code that runs at start-up, or in a lazy holder. One question from the start is still open: how can a class with a familiar name be a stranger?

try.title: Deadlock two classes
steps: Run InitDeadlockDemo (or the Kotlin twin). It starts two threads, one that needs Cast and one that needs Costumes, and waits one second.
Read the state and the top frame it prints for each thread, and what the deadlock detector says.
Optional: run it with -Pargs=wait, then run the printed jstack command in a second terminal and search for Class initialization monitor.
Fix it: make Costumes.COUNT a constant (static final long COUNT = 36; with no static block, or const val COUNT = 36L in Kotlin) and run it again.

code.title: InitDeadlockDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.bytecode.l01; import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory; import java.util.List; /** Two static initializers that need each other, started from two threads. */ public class InitDeadlockDemo { static class Cast { static final long ACTORS; static { pause(); ACTORS = Costumes.COUNT / 3; } // needs Costumes: 3 costumes an actor } static class Costumes { static final long COUNT; static { pause(); COUNT = Cast.ACTORS * 3; } // needs Cast } static void pause() { try { Thread.sleep(200); } catch (InterruptedException e) { throw new RuntimeException(e); } } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { Thread a = new Thread(() -> System.out.println(Cast.ACTORS), "cast"); Thread b = new Thread(() -> System.out.println(Costumes.COUNT), "costumes"); a.setDaemon(true); // daemon, so the JVM can still exit at the end b.setDaemon(true); a.start(); b.start(); Thread.sleep(1_000); for (Thread t : List.of(a, b)) { StackTraceElement[] stack = t.getStackTrace(); // empty once the thread has ended System.out.printf("%-8s state=%s at %s%n", t.getName(), t.getState(), stack.length > 0 ? stack[0] : "(finished)"); } long[] stuck = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean().findDeadlockedThreads(); System.out.println("deadlock detector: " + (stuck == null ? "found nothing" : stuck.length + " threads")); if (args.length > 0) { // -Pargs=wait gives you 30 s to run jstack System.out.println("jstack " + ProcessHandle.current().pid() + " (search for 'Class initialization monitor')"); Thread.sleep(30_000); } } }

alt.title: InitDeadlockDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.bytecode.l01 import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory import kotlin.concurrent.thread // Two objects whose initializers need each other, started from two threads. object KCast { @JvmField val ACTORS: Long init { pausePlease(); ACTORS = KCostumes.COUNT / 3 } // needs KCostumes: 3 costumes an actor } object KCostumes { @JvmField val COUNT: Long init { pausePlease(); COUNT = KCast.ACTORS * 3 } // needs KCast } private fun pausePlease() = Thread.sleep(200) fun main(args: Array<String>) { // daemon threads, so the JVM can still exit at the end val a = thread(name = "cast", isDaemon = true) { println(KCast.ACTORS) } val b = thread(name = "costumes", isDaemon = true) { println(KCostumes.COUNT) } Thread.sleep(1_000) for (t in listOf(a, b)) { val top = t.stackTrace.firstOrNull() ?: "(finished)" // empty once the thread has ended println("%-8s state=%s at %s".format(t.name, t.state, top)) } val stuck = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean().findDeadlockedThreads() println("deadlock detector: " + (stuck?.let { "${it.size} threads" } ?: "found nothing")) if (args.isNotEmpty()) { // -Pargs=wait gives you 30 s to run jstack println("jstack ${ProcessHandle.current().pid()} (search for 'Class initialization monitor')") Thread.sleep(30_000) } }

try.expect: Both threads show state=RUNNABLE with a top frame inside a <clinit>, and the detector prints found nothing. The JVM exits only because the threads are daemons, threads it doesn't wait for. In jstack each thread is in Object.wait() and waiting on the Class initialization monitor for the other class. After the fix, Cast reads a constant and no longer needs Costumes to initialize, so the threads print 12 and 36, both show state=TERMINATED at (finished), and the program ends normally.

sections.h: Same drawing, two stage managers: one class defined twice
sections.html:
Because the loader is part of a class's identity, a loader of your own can define a second copy of a class the app loader already has. Programs that load plugins, pieces of code added after the program was built, do this on purpose. Our show program loads each scene as a plugin. If every plugin gets its own copy of its classes, two plugins can't trip over each other's statics.

The usual tool is a child-first loader. For names in its own package it calls findClass before it asks its parent, and for everything else it delegates as usual:

Java
@Override
protected Class<?> loadClass(String name, boolean resolve) throws ClassNotFoundException {
    synchronized (getClassLoadingLock(name)) {
        Class<?> c = findLoadedClass(name);
        if (c == null && name.startsWith(prefix)) c = findClass(name);   // child-first
        return c != null ? c : super.loadClass(name, resolve);            // parent-first
    }
}
Kotlin
override fun loadClass(name: String, resolve: Boolean): Class<*> =
    synchronized(getClassLoadingLock(name)) {
        var c = findLoadedClass(name)
        if (c == null && name.startsWith(prefix)) c = findClass(name)   // child-first
        c ?: super.loadClass(name, resolve)                              // parent-first
    }

Read it as "mine first, then my parent's". The lock from getClassLoadingLock stops two threads from defining the same class twice, and findLoadedClass returns the copy this loader already made.

Two such loaders over one class file give you two Class objects. Each has its own statics, and its static initializer runs once per loader. Here the theatre picture breaks, and it's worth saying out loud. Two crowns made from the same drawing are as good as each other: any actor can wear either. Two classes defined from the same bytes are strangers. An object of one can't be cast to the other, even though the names match.

TwoLoadersDemo in the Try it loads a small Counter class through two child-first loaders. It calls hit() twice on the copy from plugin-1, then casts that object to the app loader's Counter. On JDK 25 it printed:

same name: true
c1 == c2: false, c1 == Counter.class: false
hits: plugin-1=2, plugin-2=0, app=0
class ...TwoLoadersDemo$Counter cannot be cast to class ...TwoLoadersDemo$Counter
(...$Counter is in unnamed module of loader 'plugin-1' @626b2d4a;
 ...$Counter is in unnamed module of loader 'app')

Three classes, and three separate hits fields. The cast message is long, but it's worth learning to read. The same name twice, with two loaders in the parentheses, means two copies, not a missing jar.

The two "not found" errors fit the same picture. ClassNotFoundException is a checked exception from a lookup by name that your code asked for, with Class.forName or loadClass: someone asked for a prop that nobody has. NoClassDefFoundError comes from the JVM itself, while it links or initializes code that was compiled against the class. Either the class is missing at run time (the error's cause is then a ClassNotFoundException), or its static initializer already failed, as in the last section.

Leaks have the same shape. A loader stays alive as long as anything reachable points at one of its classes or objects. In one experiment for this track, a plugin object was added to a static list in a registry that the parent loader had loaded. That one entry kept the plugin's whole URLClassLoader alive after close() and ten System.gc() calls, along with a 10 MB static array. (URLClassLoader is the JDK's loader for folders and jars, and System.gc() asks the garbage collector, the part of the JVM that frees unused memory, to run.) Without the registration, the loader was collected.

The same name with two loaders is two classes. Read both loader names in the message.

That's the whole journey of a class, from fetching its bytes to its first run. What we haven't seen yet is what those bytes say.

try.title: Two Counters that aren't the same class
steps: Read TwoLoadersDemo. It loads Counter through two child-first loaders and calls hit() twice on the copy from plugin-1.
Predict the three hits values, and whether the cast at the end works.
Run it (or the Kotlin twin) and find the two loader names in the exception message.

code.title: TwoLoadersDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.bytecode.l01; import java.io.IOException; import java.io.InputStream; /** The same class file defined by two loaders: two classes, two sets of statics. */ public class TwoLoadersDemo { public static class Counter { public static int hits; public int hit() { return ++hits; } } /** Defines Counter itself (child-first); asks the parent for everything else. */ static class ChildFirst extends ClassLoader { ChildFirst(String name) { super(name, TwoLoadersDemo.class.getClassLoader()); } @Override protected Class<?> loadClass(String name, boolean resolve) throws ClassNotFoundException { if (!name.equals(Counter.class.getName())) return super.loadClass(name, resolve); synchronized (getClassLoadingLock(name)) { Class<?> c = findLoadedClass(name); if (c != null) return c; try (InputStream in = getParent().getResourceAsStream(name.replace('.', '/') + ".class")) { byte[] bytes = in.readAllBytes(); return defineClass(name, bytes, 0, bytes.length); } catch (IOException e) { throw new ClassNotFoundException(name, e); } } } } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { String name = Counter.class.getName(); Class<?> c1 = new ChildFirst("plugin-1").loadClass(name); Class<?> c2 = new ChildFirst("plugin-2").loadClass(name); System.out.println("same name: " + c1.getName().equals(c2.getName())); System.out.println("c1 == c2: " + (c1 == c2) + ", c1 == Counter.class: " + (c1 == Counter.class)); Object fromPlugin1 = c1.getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance(); c1.getMethod("hit").invoke(fromPlugin1); c1.getMethod("hit").invoke(fromPlugin1); System.out.printf("hits: plugin-1=%s, plugin-2=%s, app=%s%n", c1.getField("hits").get(null), c2.getField("hits").get(null), Counter.hits); try { Counter c = (Counter) fromPlugin1; // checkcast against the app loader's Counter } catch (ClassCastException e) { System.out.println(e.getMessage()); } } }

alt.title: TwoLoadersDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.bytecode.l01 class KCounter { fun hit(): Int = ++hits companion object { @JvmField var hits = 0 } } /** Defines KCounter itself (child-first); asks the parent for everything else. */ private class KChildFirst(name: String) : ClassLoader(name, KCounter::class.java.classLoader) { override fun loadClass(name: String, resolve: Boolean): Class<*> { if (name != KCounter::class.java.name) return super.loadClass(name, resolve) synchronized(getClassLoadingLock(name)) { findLoadedClass(name)?.let { return it } val bytes = parent.getResourceAsStream(name.replace('.', '/') + ".class")!!.use { it.readAllBytes() } return defineClass(name, bytes, 0, bytes.size) } } } /** The same class file defined by two loaders: two classes, two sets of statics. */ fun main() { val name = KCounter::class.java.name val c1 = KChildFirst("plugin-1").loadClass(name) val c2 = KChildFirst("plugin-2").loadClass(name) println("same name: ${c1.name == c2.name}") println("c1 == c2: ${c1 == c2}, c1 == KCounter::class.java: ${c1 == KCounter::class.java}") val fromPlugin1 = c1.getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance() repeat(2) { c1.getMethod("hit").invoke(fromPlugin1) } println("hits: plugin-1=${c1.getField("hits").get(null)}, plugin-2=${c2.getField("hits").get(null)}, app=${KCounter.hits}") try { val c = fromPlugin1 as KCounter // checkcast against the app loader's KCounter } catch (e: ClassCastException) { println(e.message) } }

try.expect: same name: true, c1 == c2: false and c1 == Counter.class: false. The hits are plugin-1=2, plugin-2=0, app=0: three classes, three separate static fields. The cast fails with ... cannot be cast to class ...$Counter, and the parentheses name loader 'plugin-1' and loader 'app'. The number after the @ changes from run to run.

aside.title: Where will I meet several class loaders?
aside.html: Anywhere a program runs code it didn't start with. Application servers, programs that host several web applications at once, give each application its own loader, so two applications can use different versions of one library. Test runners and build tools often load your classes in a loader of their own. Quarkus, a framework for writing Java web services, uses several loaders in its tests and in its dev mode: your classes live in a loader that is thrown away and rebuilt on every reload, on top of one that stays. Its class-loading guide warns that marking a library "parent first" without also marking the libraries it uses can cause a LinkageError. That detail comes from the Quarkus docs; this track didn't run dev mode.

compare.title: When static initialization runs, in Java and Kotlin

java.title: Limits.java
java.html: class Limits { static final int MAX_CAST = 12; // constant: copied into callers, no init static final Integer CAP = 12; // not a constant: reading it runs <clinit> static Limits defaults() { return new Limits(); } static { System.out.println("Limits init"); } } // Limits.MAX_CAST -> nothing // Limits.CAP -> "Limits init" // Limits.defaults() -> "Limits init" (if not done yet)

kotlin.title: Limits.kt
kotlin.html: object Limits { const val MAX_CAST = 12 // constant: copied into callers, no init val CAP: Int = 12 // private static field + getCAP() on the object fun defaults() = Limits init { println("Limits init") } } // Limits.MAX_CAST -> nothing // Limits.CAP -> "Limits init" (goes through Limits.INSTANCE) // Limits.defaults() -> "Limits init" (if not done yet)

compare.note: Kotlin has no static, but an object compiles to a class with a public static final INSTANCE field and a static initializer that builds it, so the JVM's rules are the same. Only const val (primitives and String) is copied into callers like a Java constant variable. A plain val in an object becomes a private static field plus a getter, so reading it touches the class and runs its init blocks. Companion objects follow the same rules, and their init code lands in the outer class's static initializer. That's why the Kotlin CallSheet in the section on the dress rehearsal reads 0 exactly like the Java one: a quick run of it printed VIOLIN: 0.

worked.title: Read a NoClassDefFoundError back to its cause

steps.say: A test run of the show program prints this forty times. Before you read on, decide: is a jar missing?
steps.code:
java.lang.NoClassDefFoundError: Could not initialize class theatre.ScriptBook
    at theatre.Rehearsals.start(Rehearsals.java:31)
    ...
Caused by: java.lang.ExceptionInInitializerError: Exception java.lang.IllegalStateException:
    script file missing: hamlet.txt [in thread "main"]

steps.say: No. "Could not initialize class" means the JVM found ScriptBook and already tried its static initializer once. The cause (JDK 21 and later) points at that first failure. Here is the class. Every static field initializer is a line of <clinit>, run once, in order.
steps.code: public final class ScriptBook { // 1. runs inside <clinit>: any exception here poisons the class for good static final ScriptBook CURRENT = load(Path.of("hamlet.txt")); static ScriptBook load(Path p) { if (!Files.exists(p)) throw new IllegalStateException("script file missing: " + p); return new ScriptBook(/* read 4,000 lines */); } }

alt.html: class ScriptBook private constructor() { companion object { // 1. runs inside ScriptBook's <clinit>: any exception here poisons the class for good val CURRENT: ScriptBook = load(Path.of("hamlet.txt")) fun load(p: Path): ScriptBook { check(Files.exists(p)) { "script file missing: $p" } return ScriptBook(/* read 4,000 lines */) } } }

steps.say: Move the file reading out of class initialization, into an ordinary object that the program builds once at start-up. If the file is missing, start-up fails once, with a clear stack trace, and the next run after the file is fixed simply works. The class has no static state left to poison.
steps.code: public final class Scripts { private final ScriptBook current; public Scripts(Path file) { current = ScriptBook.load(file); // 2. ordinary code, ordinary exception } public ScriptBook current() { return current; } // 3. no static state left to poison } // at start-up, once: Scripts scripts = new Scripts(Path.of("hamlet.txt"));

alt.html: class Scripts(file: Path) { private val current: ScriptBook = ScriptBook.load(file) // 2. ordinary code, ordinary exception fun current(): ScriptBook = current // 3. no static state left to poison } // at start-up, once: val scripts = Scripts(Path.of("hamlet.txt"))

steps.say: If the value must stay static, make it lazy with a holder class (memory model track, lesson 5). A failure still poisons the holder, but only callers that need the script see it, and the error appears at the first real use instead of whenever some unrelated code touched ScriptBook.

lab.title: Fix the call sheet, then load one class twice
steps: Run the tests once. Eight of ten fail: an unlisted role gets 0 minutes instead of 60, and every loader test hits UnsupportedOperationException.

In CallSheet, read the static fields from top to bottom, the way <clinit> runs them. Move one line so the constructor sees the real DEFAULT_MINUTES. Don't change any number. Ask yourself why unit() was right all along.

IsolatingLoader is a child-first loader for the show program's scene plugins. In its findClass, read the class file through the parent with getParent().getResourceAsStream(name.replace('.', '/') + ".class"), then call defineClass(name, bytes, 0, bytes.length). Throw ClassNotFoundException when the stream is null.

In loadClass, take getClassLoadingLock(name). Return findLoadedClass(name) if it isn't null. For names that start with the prefix, call findClass. For everything else, return super.loadClass(name, resolve).
Run the tests until all ten pass. Then read castAcrossLoadersFails and find which loader names appear in the message.
hints: Constants such as "minutes" are copied into the code by javac, so their order doesn't matter. Integer.parseInt(...) is a method call, so DEFAULT_MINUTES is 0 until <clinit> reaches its line.
If a test fails with LinkageError: attempted duplicate class definition, your loadClass defined the same name twice. Check findLoadedClass first.
Don't call super.loadClass for prefix names before findClass: the parent would find the app's copy, and you'd get the same Class from both loaders.

drill.title: A child-first loader from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page and the lab. Write loadClass(String name, boolean resolve) for a loader that defines classes under prefix itself and asks its parent for everything else. Then check: did you take the class-loading lock, and did you look for an already-loaded class before defining one?

answer.html: @Override protected Class<?> loadClass(String name, boolean resolve) throws ClassNotFoundException { synchronized (getClassLoadingLock(name)) { Class<?> c = findLoadedClass(name); // 1. defined here already? if (c == null && name.startsWith(prefix)) { c = findClass(name); // 2. child-first for the plugin } if (c == null) return super.loadClass(name, resolve); // 3. parent-first for the rest if (resolve) resolveClass(c); return c; } }

alt.html: override fun loadClass(name: String, resolve: Boolean): Class<*> = synchronized(getClassLoadingLock(name)) { var c = findLoadedClass(name) // 1. defined here already? if (c == null && name.startsWith(prefix)) { c = findClass(name) // 2. child-first for the plugin } if (c == null) return super.loadClass(name, resolve) // 3. parent-first for the rest if (resolve) resolveClass(c) c }

recap: Three built-in loaders: bootstrap (null, java.base), platform (the other JDK modules) and app (your class path). Each asks its parent first, so the JDK's classes can't be replaced.
A class is (binary name, defining loader). The same bytes defined by two loaders are two classes with separate statics, and casts between them fail with both loader names in the message.

Loading, linking (verify, prepare, resolve) and initialization are separate and lazy. Only initialization runs <clinit>, on first real use: new, a static call, a non-constant static read or write, reflection, a subclass.

<clinit> runs once, top to bottom, under a lock. A throw gives ExceptionInInitializerError once, then NoClassDefFoundError: Could not initialize class forever. Two initializers that need each other can deadlock with both threads RUNNABLE.
ClassNotFoundException is a lookup by name that failed. NoClassDefFoundError is the JVM failing to link or initialize a class your code was compiled against.
The limit: loaders and initialization rules tell you when a class arrives and when its start-up code runs, not what the compiled code actually does. For that you read the bytecode.

explain.prompt: A teammate sees NoClassDefFoundError: Could not initialize class CallSheet in a running program and wants to add call-sheet.jar to the class path. Explain what the error really says, how you'd find the cause, and how to stop it happening again.
explain.answer: The JVM found CallSheet fine. It already tried to run its static initializer once, that initializer threw, and the JVM marked the class as failed, so every later use gets NoClassDefFoundError and it never tries again. Adding a jar won't help. I'd look for the first ExceptionInInitializerError in the log, or read the error's cause, which since JDK 21 names the original exception and the thread. The fix is whatever made the initializer throw, plus moving that work out of <clinit>: keep statics to constants and small fixed tables, and do file reading or configuration in ordinary code that runs at start-up, or in a lazy holder, so a failure is an ordinary exception at the call that needs it.

deeper.html:
Three details that didn't fit above.

Interfaces have their own initialization rule. Initializing a class initializes its superclass, but its superinterfaces only if they declare a default method. In one experiment, new Impl() for a class implementing WithDefault (which has a default method) and NoDefault (which doesn't) printed WithDefault.<clinit> and Impl.<clinit>, and NoDefault stayed uninitialized until code read one of its fields. HotSpot's InstanceKlass::initialize_impl follows the specification's steps one by one, and its comments quote this rule.

Lambdas are hidden classes. A lambda's class has a name like InitDeadlockDemo$$Lambda/0x0000000055080210 (a full jstack of the deadlock demo shows two such frames), isHidden() returns true, and Class.forName on that name throws ClassNotFoundException. LambdaMetafactory defines it with Lookup.defineHiddenClass (JDK 15) as a nestmate of the class that contains the lambda, which means it may use that class's private members. Lesson 3 of this track shows the call that creates it.

You can watch the steps happen. -Xlog:class+load=info prints a line for each loaded class with where it came from, and -Xlog:class+init=info prints when verification starts and ends and an Initializing '...' line for each class. A Hello World with one lambda loaded 560 classes on JDK 21 and 645 on JDK 25, most of them from the CDS archive (source: shared objects file), a file of JDK classes that were already parsed when the JDK was built. The startup track covers that archive and the AOT cache that JDK 24 and 25 build on it.

java -Xlog:class+load=info -Xlog:class+init=info -cp bytecode/build/classes/java/demo workbench.bytecode.l01.InitPuzzle | grep -E 'InitPuzzle|Initializing'
